Messages.Author: Sten During
Messages.Body:
Why groups working in tandem with vampires at all?

What's the rationale behind grouping Imbued so that
they may not be played together with any vampire?

Grouping, if I have understood it correctly, was
implemented to avoid the dial-a-crypt problem, which
I think is a good thing.
From the preview the Imbued would seem to work along
mechanisms different from vampires so a group 4
imbued should pose exactly the same problem with
vampires from groups 3 - 5 as with vampires from
groups 1 - 2.
Disabling a group 1 Imbued from being in the same
crypt as a group 4 Imbued is perfectly understandable,
but preventing a group 4 Imbued from being in a crypt
together with a group 1 vampire has no rationale. Unless,
of course, "it's easier avoiding confusion this way" is
the rationale.

I personally don't see "making it easier" as a valid
rationale here -- especially as NoR introduces even
more stuff to remember to begin with :)

Why not keep groups within scope of type of crypt-
minions? Ie, Vampires, Imbued, future Mages, Garous,
Mummies and whatnot don't carry over their group-
designations in a mixed crypt.

Sten During

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <44280167$0$18319$6d36...@titian.nntpserver.com>, Sten

During <ya...@netg.se> writes:
>Groups where explicitly introduced to avoid "optimal" sharing
>of disciplines, or to take it to the extreme, to disable the
>making of a crypt with twelve identical vampires differing
>in name only.

See, this is where you fall down.

When rules are changed, it doesn't have to be to satisfy one criterion
and one criterion only. Rules being what they are, they very often have
a variety of knock-on effects, at least some of which can be intended.

So, crypt grouping does achieve the effect of disabling twelve identical
vampires in a crypt with exactly the same disciplines - particularly
when they're weenie vampires. But it doesn't just do that.

Crypt grouping also achieves an interesting way of allowing flexibility
with clans, whilst keeping each clan from becoming the same as all the
others - Presence Ravnos in 3/4, Fortitude Giovanni in 3/4, but you
can't suddenly amass a few dozen of "out of clan" disciplines on a
clutch of vampires within a clan so that you get a deck with 12 Ventrue
Vicissitude users; both Ventrue and the Vicissitude discipline retain
distinct flavours, whilst allowing them both to try out new things. But
it doesn't just do that.

Crypt grouping achieves a way of improving accessibility for new
players. Across two or three expansions / base sets / whatever, they
can get all the cards they need for the crypt of their choice. They
don't need to go hunting for old, out-of-print vampires on Ebay, and
oldbies don't have super-optimized crypts. Note that super-optimized
doesn't necessarily mean 12 identical vampires. But it doesn't just
improve accessibility for newbies.

No-one would deny that it's also a useful sales ploy for White Wolf,
without being an egregious cash-cow. It helps keep people buying so
that they can exploit all their new toys, whilst not actively causing
oldbies to have to buy new cards, except in as far as printing any new
cards (library cards in particular) may cause them to want to buy new
cards to make an old solid deck slightly more competitive. But it
doesn't just do that.

Crypt grouping requires you to put in effort to maximise the
possibilities for a given deck. Every new vampire printed without
groups is a slightly easier choice for deck builders. This way, deck
building remains a challenge. But it doesn't just do that.

If you think crypt grouping is ONLY about twelve identical vampires in a
crypt, you're wrong. And arguments based on it only being about twelve
identical vampires are shaky as a result.

>I have players here who wonder what the rationale is. The
>only rationale I can give is "Because it's the lazy way to
>solve it.", and unsurprisingly enough that is not a valid
>enough argument.

See, the flip-side of laziness is consistency.

Why add another rule? Why have to explain to players "Well, all your
cards should have the a number there that's 1 or 2, 2 or 3, 3 or 4, or 4
or 5, but never 1 and 4. Oh, except when it's imbued when you can break
that." Why make the exception, rather than sticking to the rule? As it
stands, it's nice and easy to explain - ALL CRYPT CARDS, TWO CONSECUTIVE
GROUPS.

Overly delicate rules have been got rid of in the past to streamline
areas where the fiddling isn't necessary - paralyse, close quarters,
archbishops rushing princes, etc. This could be considered much the
same - avoiding unnecessary complication.

--
James Coupe

with group 6 vampires enters the game we'll have two sets of vampires
unmixable with Imbueds (assuming no more Imbueds in any significicant

the game will encounter a situation when they're able to buy an old
expansion and have two mutually exclusive sets of cards -- library cards
as well as crypt cards. This is a BAD (tm) situation, and one that the
design team currently have avoided.

Allowing "crypt minions" of different types to mix no matter groupings
but still be limited by groupings within scope of each type would
limit the need for adding token "crypt minions" to expansions in order
to ensure that "all" (as in the VAST majority) library cards may always
be legal to play.

If I'm a new player five years in the future who for some reason got
my hands upon half a display-box of NoR I'd be extremely disappointed
if I was told that each and every card of those 18 boosters were
wallpaper and unmixable with the four full display-boxes I bought
recently. The reason I bought those 18 booster packs was that I was
told that I'll always be able to use library cards even though there
may be limitations to which vampires I may have in any one given crypt.

Anyone familiar with me knows that I'm normally in favour of the rules
in the game. That includes the grouping rule in general. Sure, a few
cards have met with my disapproval, but hey, I'm only human.
In this case, however, I see problems further along the line rather than
when NoR hits the shelves, which I adressed above.

such as group 2/3, can still have access to 6 Bloodlines vampires, but
you have 3 in each group, and can then add 3 to group 4 and end up with
some interesting cross-overs, and 3 in group 5. And so in groups 2 to 5
you still have the same number you'd get before - roughly 12 - and you
get all six at each end, but you also get a cross-over in the middle.

Also, the Laibon have been spread over 3 and 4, not just 4.

- that LSJ may be purposefully not creating so many Hunters so that, if
he wants to, he can add more in Group 5 once he has an idea of how
players react to them, etc.

playtesting then becomes a mess;

twinkers who think the grouping rule has no reason to exist;

good enough; by that broken logic, murder should be allowed by law
because it's commited everywhere, and so on)

All this just to allow more combinations, when all the rest of the
crypt cards combinations are restricted in some way. Too much trouble
for little gain, I'd say.

> - it's one more thing to complicate even further a game that's already
> complicated (and no, the argument "but it's complicated already" is not
> good enough; by that broken logic, murder should be allowed by law
> because it's commited everywhere, and so on)

The added complication introduced with scoped groups is as I see it both
a minor one and a VERY minor one compared to the benefits.

>
> All this just to allow more combinations, when all the rest of the
> crypt cards combinations are restricted in some way. Too much trouble
> for little gain, I'd say.
>

The main gain is focus. This is from a game-constructing point of view.
Scoped groups removes the need for splashing in "creatures" in each and
every expansion in order to keep up access to "creatures" for each group
of "other creatures", in which I include vampires. Just make a set with
whatever theme you had in mind and be sure that the main actors will be
mixable with everything already out there, provided of course there's no
illegal scoped group mixing.

The second gain is flexibility for the future of the game. You don't
want to buy all cards, and for some reason prefer avoiding vampires.
Mages are cool, and mixable with the minions from this old set NoR.
Assuming that this game will continue to focus on vampires it's a lot
easier making the odd set of "creatures" now and then and more or less
leave them out of set-design when you make a new vampire-based
expansion.

The third, admittedly short term, gain is renewal of player-base. I
agree that this is a weak one, but anyway. Old players on hiatus since
Final Nights or older who are curious with this VERY new addition to the
game can just buy a box and get going with their existing stock of
cards.
